name: Flatpack — drop a manual PDF, get a step-by-step build card
one_liner: For anyone sitting on the floor with a wordless assembly manual, Flatpack turns the PDF into a scrollable step card deck: each step in plain English, the exact parts and screws for that step with counts, the tool you need, and the panel from the manual blown up beside it.
problem: Everyone who has assembled flat-pack furniture, a bike, a crib or a gas grill has squinted at a wordless diagram trying to work out whether that screw is the 15mm or the 20mm, and which of the eight identical-looking boards is panel D. The manual is a 12-page PDF of silent pictures; the human has to hold the whole sequence in their head, keeps losing their place, and discovers at step 9 that step 4 was backwards. People currently cope by zooming into a phone PDF, pausing a YouTube video from a stranger's garage, or asking a chat app one photo at a time. What is tedious: the mapping between the hardware baggie and the diagram, and knowing what each step actually accomplishes. Flatpack does the whole manual at once and gives a checklist you can tick as you go, with a hardware tally at the top so you know before you start whether you are missing a cam lock.
target_customer: Consumers and weekend DIYers assembling flat-pack furniture, bikes, cribs and grills; reachable on X, r/ikea, r/DIY and TikTok. Free and open source, no signup.
why_now: Gemini 3 Pro Image / Nano Banana Pro (and GPT Image 2-class models) can now read multi-panel wordless diagrams and render legible annotated callouts — labelled technical illustration with readable text was unreliable a year ago, and this is exactly the capability a popular bookmark (@nutlope's 'I'm never reading IKEA instructions again', 11k likes) and the /teardown skill (@jakubkrehel, 5.1k likes) are both riding. The research layer caught up too: the IKEA-Manual dataset (102 items, 393 annotated steps) and the 2026 IKEA-Bench and M2AD benchmarks exist for checking step extraction. API cost is real but small: Gemini 3 Pro Image is $0.134 per 1K/2K output image, ~$0.067 batched; a text/vision pass over a 12-page manual is cents.
comparables: ScrewYouIKEA (devpost.com/software/screwyouikea) — a hackathon prototype doing PDF → 3D animated steps with PDF.js, Gemini and Three.js; ambitious, not maintained, not a usable web app. TalkingPDF and ManualScout — chat-with-your-manual tools (ManualScout is iPhone-only, 50 free questions/day); they answer questions but never produce a structured, tickable step list with a per-step hardware tally. IKEA's own assembly videos cover only selected products. The /teardown skill makes a technical illustration of an object; Flatpack goes the other direction — it consumes an existing manual and outputs a procedure, for a non-developer audience with no CLI. It also differs from the library's Partsy (one photo → one labelled exploded diagram of an unfamiliar object): Flatpack takes a multi-page document, not a photo, and its output is an ordered, checkable build sequence with a hardware inventory, not a single annotated picture.
risks: 1) One-time toy: you assemble a bookcase twice a year, so weekly return visits are unlikely — the counter is breadth (bikes, grills, cribs, appliances, LEGO-adjacent kits, machine manuals) and a shareable output, but retention will stay the weak score. 2) Accuracy on genuinely wordless diagrams is the whole product; if the model miscounts screws or inverts a step, the user is worse off than with the original — mitigated by always showing the real cropped panel beside the generated text and labelling uncertain hardware. 3) Prior art risk from a big player: IKEA or a model vendor could ship 'point your camera at the manual' natively, and @nutlope's own bookmarked demo suggests others are already circling this exact idea.
build_plan: Stack: single Next.js page on Vercel, no database, no auth. (1) Client-side PDF.js renders each manual page to a PNG at ~1500px. (2) Send all pages in one Gemini 3 Pro (text+vision) call with a strict JSON schema: steps[] { n, title, plain_english, parts:[{label, count}], hardware:[{label, count, size}], tool, page, panel_bbox, warning }. (3) Crop each step's panel from the rendered page using panel_bbox and show it beside the text — real pixels from the real manual, so nothing is hallucinated visually. (4) Render as a swipeable card deck with a checkbox per step, a sticky 'hardware you'll need' tally computed from the JSON, and a progress bar; persist ticks in localStorage so you can put the phone down. (5) Ship with 4 preloaded demo manuals (an IKEA bookcase, a bike, a grill, an office chair) so the page is instantly playable with no upload. (6) 'Share this build' button renders the step deck to a long PNG. Cut for v1: 3D rendering, camera-based 'am I on step 5' detection, voice, accounts, any manual library/scraping, multi-language. Cost control: cap at 20 pages, one model call per manual, hash the file client-side to reuse cached demo results.
launch_post: Drop in any flat-pack manual PDF. Flatpack reads the wordless diagrams and gives you back real steps: what each one does, exactly which screws and how many, the tool you need, and the panel blown up next to it. Tick them off as you go. Free, open source, no signup.
reasoning: Won the build track because it is the only candidate where the input is something everyone physically has, the output is obviously better than the original in under ten seconds, and every dependency checked out: PDF.js is free, the panel crops come from the user's own file rather than a generated image, and Gemini 3 Pro Image/vision pricing at $0.134 per output image means a full manual costs cents. It matches the taste file's pattern exactly — one input, a striking result, free and open source, demo-able in a single screenshot. It loses a point on usefulness because assembly is infrequent, and it is deliberately scoped away from the library's Partsy (photo → one diagram) by taking a document and emitting an ordered, tickable procedure with a hardware tally. Beat the agent-config visualiser (too close to the library's Skillscope and to developers again) and the thread-to-decision-log tool (ThreadSummary, Sotto and AI Emaily already do it free, and it shares the venture's audience and theme).
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Ledgerline — billable-work evidence trail for small agencies and consultancies. KEPT and selected: confirmed gap between quote-only enterprise passive timekeepers (Laurel, Smokeball AutoTime) and $10-25/seat agency PSA tools that only work if you logged it at the time; buyer owns the invoice.
2. Agent attribution layer for shared email/calendar ("who did what" across personal agents, from @sriramk). DROPPED: Google is shipping per-agent identities with their own Workspace accounts and audit trails, Gmail/Calendar APIs expose no creating-OAuth-client field, and the whole category is being absorbed by Workspace/Entra plus shadow-AI governance vendors (Push, Obsidian, Token Security). Also too close to the library's Driftwatch and Holdroom in buyer and theme.
3. Consent evidence vault for Messenger/SMS brand campaigns (from the Blueberry Broadcasts post + one-to-one consent rules). DROPPED as a lead: ActiveProspect TrustedForm already sells exactly this artifact at $0.15/certificate with a $10/mo self-serve minimum, and the platforms (Shopify Messaging, Attentive) do the pre-send screening — a well-funded player serving the same buyer with the same workflow at a fair price. Its evidence-artifact business model was carried over as the analogue for Ledgerline.
4. Agent-action reconciliation for clinic/home-services PMS and CRM records. DROPPED: real pain found (no vendor clearly demonstrates conflict detection or rollback for competing agent/staff edits), but it requires deep per-PMS integrations with Eaglesoft, eClinicalWorks and ServiceTitan — far past a solo builder's narrow first version, and the wedge would take months before one buyer could try it.

BUILD
1. Flatpack — manual PDF → tickable step deck with per-step hardware. KEPT and selected: dependencies all check out (PDF.js free, panels cropped from the user's own file, Gemini 3 Pro Image at $0.134/image, IKEA-Manual and IKEA-Bench datasets exist for validation); closest prior art is an unmaintained hackathon demo (ScrewYouIKEA) and chat-with-PDF tools that never produce a structured procedure.
2. Agent-config X-ray — paste an instructions.md / AGENTS.md / Cursor Agent SDK project and see the tool graph and capability surface. DROPPED as a repeat-adjacent: same audience and same core workflow as the library's Skillscope (paste an agent config, get a one-screen read on what it can do), just a different filename.
3. Thread → decision log: paste an email thread, get a dated record of what was agreed and by whom. DROPPED: good free versions already exist and are easy to find (ThreadSummary's 5 free summaries/month, Sotto's free notes generator, AI Emaily), and it shares its theme and audience with the Ledgerline venture, which the two-different-problems rule forbids.
4. Public dataset as a browsable shelf (taste-file pattern). DROPPED: I could not verify a specific fresh dataset that would make it newly possible this week, so freshness would score low and it would be a pretty page with no 'why now'.
research_notes:
22-call budget, 20 used. Reading pot (3/3): summarised supermemory's learner-1 (a cross-model memory layer, not weight-level continual learning — which killed my first read of that bookmark), the Cursor Agent SDK launch (markdown instructions + TypeScript tools + built-in evals + GitHub/Slack event triggers), and Blueberry Social Broadcasts (the 'upload your email list, find their Messenger profiles' claim is not confirmed on the vendor's own site, and Meta requires opt-in for marketing messages — so I treated the post as a prompt about consent evidence rather than a model to copy). I cannot see images; all three of those posts were video-only, so the summaries did the work.

Venture pot (11/12): searched agent identity/audit for email and calendar, which showed Google shipping per-agent Workspace identities (Oct 2026) and confirmed via the Calendar/Gmail API docs that no field exposes the creating OAuth client — this killed candidate 2 outright. Searched shadow-AI governance (Push, Obsidian, Token Security, Guardz) and found the enterprise end well covered. Researched TCPA one-to-one consent and found ActiveProspect TrustedForm's published pricing ($0.15/certificate, $10/mo minimum), which closed candidate 3 but gave me the evidence-artifact analogue I used in Ledgerline's comparables. Probed multi-agent ops pain in claims/billing/logistics (stale reads, conflicting writes, hard attribution) and clinic/home-services PMS write-backs (Yourcall, Echo Booking, Flexbone, Atty — none demonstrably reconcile conflicting edits), which was real but too integration-heavy. The decisive calls were the last three: automatic time capture (Laurel quote-only and enterprise-paced; Smokeball AutoTime Windows-only with no Google Workspace support; Clio Duo at $89-149/user/mo and legal-only) and agency PSA pricing (Teamwork $9.99/$24.99, Productive ~$9-10 with a 10-seat minimum, Scoro ~$17-19.90, Accelo quote-only). Those two calls reshaped the candidate from a vague 'agent audit trail' into the specific invoice-defence wedge and set the realistic price point.

Build pot (6/7): checked IKEA/manual prior art twice — found ScrewYouIKEA (unmaintained hackathon project), TalkingPDF and ManualScout (chat interfaces, iPhone-only in one case), and confirmed no free web tool produces a structured checklist with per-step parts and tools; also confirmed IKEA publishes assembly PDFs per product page but offers no API or archive, so v1 must be upload-only. Verified model economics twice: Gemini 3 Pro Image at $0.134 per 1K/2K image ($0.067 batched), no free API tier, and Google's own warning that generated labels can be wrong — which is exactly why the build plan crops real panels from the user's PDF instead of generating diagrams. Checked exploded-view/technical-illustration prior art and found only CLI skills and CAD tools, nothing consumer. Searched agent-config visualisers and thread-to-decision-log tools, both of which turned up enough free prior art (and overlap with the library or the venture) to drop them. Net effect of the research: the venture was reshaped from agent-attribution to agency invoice evidence, and the build was reshaped from 'generate a diagram' to 'crop the real diagram and generate only the words'.
prototype_summary: A clickable Flatpack prototype where picking a demo manual runs a simulated 1.8s parse and produces a 14-step tickable BILLY bookcase build deck with hardware tally, CSS diagram panels, uncertainty chips, progress ring and a shareable poster modal.
